articles.title: Head of Arab list elected deputy speaker of Israel's parliament
articles.summary:
Head of Arab list elected deputy speaker of Israel's parliament

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 13:50
Ahmad Tibi, who served as deputy speaker between 2006 and 2022, secured the position despite facing opposition from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi speaks to supporters in Ara, northern Israel, on 23 October 2026 (Ahmad Gharabli/AFP)
Off

Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi was elected deputy speaker of Israel's parliament on Monday, securing a prominent position after parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel made significant gains in last month's election.

Tibi, who chairs the Joint List alliance and leads the Ta'al party, told Al Jazeera that his appointment was a "rightful achievement" for the alliance, which secured 11 seats in the 27 October election.

The Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra'am), which represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament, marking a significant increase in their representation.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Tibi accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir of attempting to prevent his election, saying they had failed despite what he described as "reckless incitement".

"The Joint List will be represented in all committees," he said.

Following the elections, allegations have swirled that Netanyahu and members of his office sought to undermine Arab political parties.

On Sunday, Tibi called for a criminal investigation into Netanyahu and his aides, accusing them of engaging in "mafia-style conduct" following an investigative report by Israel's Channel 12 television.

The report alleged that Netanyahu's chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the police commissioner’s office ahead of the election, claiming that three Ra’am activists in southern Israel were carrying large sums of cash and vouchers intended to influence voters.

Police subsequently raided the activists' homes and arrested them, reportedly relying on information from an intelligence source who was a former employee of the prime minister’s office. 

Palestinian parties must not help Eisenkot rescue Israel from collapse
Read More »

The report also alleged that Shin Bet chief David Zini sought permission to wiretap the phones of five Arab lawmakers on election day.

Israel's attorney general reportedly rejected the request.

"No one is above the law, not even Netanyahu," Tibi wrote on X on Sunday, calling for an investigation into the allegations. The prime minister's Likud party has denied the accusations.

Tibi, who was first elected to the Knesset in 1999, previously served as deputy speaker between 2006 and 2022. 

Several Palestinian and Arab lawmakers have held the position, including Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas, who served from 2020 to 2022.

The Joint List has backed former army chief Gadi Eisenkot in his efforts to form Israel’s next government after President Isaac Herzog tasked him with the job earlier this month.

Neither Eisenkot’s alliance nor Netanyahu’s bloc secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority, leaving the support of Arab-led parties potentially decisive in the negotiations.

articles.title: Israeli military says it will not evict settlers occupying Palestinian homes in Jericho
articles.summary:
Israeli military says it will not evict settlers occupying Palestinian homes in Jericho

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 11:53
Earlier this month, Israeli families raided a West Bank neighbourhood and took over eight Palestinian homes
Palestinian Bedouin children, whose homes near the occupied West Bank city of Jericho were taken over by Israeli settlers the previous week, play at a new location near the city limits on 9 November 2026 (AFP)
Off

The Israeli military has decided not to evacuate 13 settler families who raided Palestinian homes in a neighbourhood of Jericho in the eastern occupied West Bank, as military officials fear a right-wing backlash, the Israeli news site Walla reported on Monday.

Earlier this month, Palestinian security sources said Israeli settlers, accompanied by their families, stormed eight Palestinian homes in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, west of Jericho. The homes were empty at the time, and the settlers smashed their doors before occupying the properties, the security sources told the Wafa news agency.

Israeli rights group Peace Now said that around 30 settlers came to take over the houses, and as they did, "they assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg".

Walla reported that the raid violated army regulations and was carried out without prior military approval. However, Avi Bluth, the commander of the Israeli army in the West Bank, has decided against evicting the settlers.

With Israel's next government still being decided, Bluth wants to avoid controversial moves, the report said, including the evacuation of the settler families.

Bluth, who grew up in an Israeli settlement, has overseen policies to expand settler outposts across the West Bank during his tenure, ordered the army to block the settlers' road leading to Area A, which is under Palestinian Authority control and where Israeli law prohibits Israelis from entering.

The settlers invaded homes in Area C, where Israel maintains full civil and military control under the 1993 Oslo Accords.

An army spokesperson told Walla that the buildings raided by settlers were "illegally constructed in Area C" and were subject to demolition orders.

Although the Israeli army officially said it had no prior knowledge of the settlers' plans to raid the homes, Haaretz revealed days after the incident that Bluth had known about the planned attack but did not inform other commanders of the impending raid until the settlers had entered the homes.

'Returning to Jericho'

Almost two weeks ago, Haaretz reported that settler families had raided homes in Jericho, with settler leaders claiming the properties had been legally purchased from their Palestinian owners.

Hussein Hamayel, governor of the Jericho region, told AFP that the land in question is owned by the Palestinian Authority and cannot be sold.

"What is being promoted is a forgery, not a sale, and what is being circulated is settler propaganda," Hamayel said.

Meanwhile, Haaretz reported that some of the homes were built on Israeli "state land", a designation under a land scheme that allows Israel to take control of large areas of land in the occupied territory.

Palestinian families brace for expulsion as settlers erect outpost near West Bank village
Read More »

Therefore, the report said, the homes could not have been purchased legally, as the land is officially administered by the state.

The army spokesperson said "the Civil Administration is continuing to examine the purchase procedures" of the Palestinian homes by the settlers.

Following the raid, Palestinian families left nearby homes, fearing violent reprisals by settlers.

"They want all of Jericho," a Palestinian woman who fled her home told the Israeli independent website +972 Magazine last week, referring to the settlers.

"This is a long-term strategy; the government gives them free rein and backing to act this way. They come armed, and if anyone speaks to them, they shoot them. We're not allowed to speak."

Meanwhile, on Sunday, two Israeli lawmakers from the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, visited the settler families, with both vowing to repeal the Oslo Accords.

MP Limor Son Har Melech posted a video of her visit to the illegal settlement, saying on X that "the struggle to cancel the Oslo Accords is being waged in the Knesset and on the ground".

"We are returning to Jericho, and with God's help we will soon, in our days, return to the Gaza area as well," she added.

MP Hanamel Dorfman, who accompanied Son Har Melech, meanwhile, said on X that "the pioneering families settling in Jericho are writing a new chapter" in the effort to cancel the Oslo Accords.

"Every home that is settled and every family that makes its home in Jericho changes the reality and strengthens the Jewish hold on the land," the newly elected lawmaker said, adding that his party "will give the families our full backing".

More than 500,000 Israeli settlers live in illegal settlements in the West Bank, which is home to over three million Palestinians.

articles.title: Britain's definition of 'anti-Muslim hostility' protects the state, not those being targeted
articles.summary:
Britain's definition of 'anti-Muslim hostility' protects the state, not those being targeted

Submitted by Karsen Trull on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 14:09
New report from Cage International shows how UK policy leaves the central mechanism of post-9/11 Islamophobia untouched - and lends it official cover
Britain's definition of anti-Muslim hostility 'is not a failed attempt to protect Muslims. It is a successful attempt to protect the state' (Reuters)
Off

This year marked a quarter of a century since the beginning of the “war on terror”, and in that time, the British state has built one of the most extensive counter-extremism systems in the world. 

Also this year, Britain produced - for the first time - an official definition of what it calls “anti-Muslim hostility”. It would be easy to treat these as separate stories, one about security and the other about community relations - but a new report from Cage International argues that they are not. 

The definition has been shaped so precisely around the security state that, read closely, it functions less as a protection for Muslims than as a protection for the institutions that have spent two decades treating them as suspects.

The key, as the report sets out, lies in a single word that runs through every part of the definition: intent. Anti-Muslim hostility, as the government defines it, means intentionally engaging in criminal acts against Muslims, or stereotyping them “with the intention of encouraging hatred.” It means discrimination where the conduct “is intended to disadvantage Muslims in public and economic life”. 

Discrimination rarely announces itself this way. The Islamophobia Response Unit, a charity that handles discrimination casework, has warned that the threshold excludes most of the cases it sees: bias, institutional barriers, and recruitment processes that quietly filter out applicants with Muslim names. 

Professor Nasar Meer of the University of Glasgow has identified the omission of the systemic and structural as the definition’s central weakness. Amina Easat-Daas, a politics lecturer at De Montfort University in Leicester, has warned that it creates a hierarchy of racism.

The intent requirement does more than leave victims of everyday discrimination without recourse; it draws a line around the state itself. Institutions acting under statutory duties do not, in the language of the definition, intend to encourage hatred. They are following policy, and that is exactly where the most consequential Islamophobia in Britain lives.

Dominant logic

To understand why, the report returns to how anti-Muslim prejudice changed after 2001. 

Before 9/11, the dominant logic in the West tolerated Islam in principle while treating certain Muslims, the “fundamentalist” or the insufficiently integrated, as the problem. Author Mahmood Mamdani captured this in Good Muslim, Bad Muslim, showing how dividing Muslims into moderates and extremists fed suspicion of all of them. 

After 9/11, the target moved. Islam itself came to be treated as the threat, an ideology that could be “hijacked” and weaponised. 

In a political culture where hostility towards Islam as a belief system has been the main vehicle for hostility towards Muslims for 25 years, that separation does not protect anyone

In this view, the devout, practising and politically engaged Muslim was suspect not for anything they had done, but for what they believed. Research on this period has shown how even apparently positive portrayals of Islam as a corruptible faith served to legitimise the policing of Muslim-presenting people.

The report finds that the new definition fits this logic with remarkable precision. It insists on protecting individuals rather than the religion, and explicitly safeguards the right to ridicule and insult Islam and to portray it in ways its adherents find disrespectful. 

In a political culture where hostility towards Islam as a belief system has been the main vehicle for hostility towards Muslims for 25 years, that separation does not protect anyone. It leaves the central mechanism of post-9/11 Islamophobia untouched, and lends it official cover.

We see this logic become law clearly with Prevent. Since 2015, teachers, doctors and even nursery staff have been under a statutory duty to watch for signs of “radicalisation”. The Cage report highlights that before the Home Office stopped breaking down referrals by religion, 39 percent of children referred were Muslim, in a population where Muslims make up a fraction of that share. 

The UN special rapporteur on counterterrorism found that Prevent had a discriminatory effect on Muslim communities and was inconsistent with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Not one Prevent referral made in line with the duty can be captured by a definition that demands proof of intent to stir up hatred.

Embedded racism

The wider context in which the UK’s definition was published confirms the direction of travel Cage has long documented. The “Protecting What Matters” strategy embedded the 2024 extremism definition across government, naming Islamism as a predominant threat.

It introduced new surveillance of campuses and speaker events, proposed an annual “State of Extremism” report, and gave the Charity Commission new powers to shut down organisations and remove trustees. 

A critique from the Ayaan Institute concluded that the government’s strategy embeds Islamophobia in state policy, rather than protecting Muslims from it. 

These powers follow a familiar pattern. They are justified by exploiting public fears and prejudices about Muslims - and once in place, their reach extends to students, protesters, charities, and civil society as a whole. What is built for one community becomes available for use against everyone.

The normalising of Islamophobia in UK public life is fuelling hate and violence
Read More »

This is also the context in which to understand the long-awaited appointment of a special representative on anti-Muslim hostility. Ministers graciously promised select Muslim individuals at Downing Street in late October that a name would come within the week, and none has yet appeared. 

Yet the identity of the appointee matters less than the function of the role. The government has maintained a policy of disengagement from the Muslim Council of Britain (MCB) since 2009. It barred the MCB from the consultation that produced this definition, and the council declined to endorse the result. 

A government-appointed representative tasked with implementing a definition the community did not build is not a channel for Muslim concerns. It is a way of supplying the legitimacy that the community itself has withheld. For that reason, the Cage report calls for the role to be abandoned altogether, and for the government to engage instead with organisations that have long records of serving their communities.

Seen in this light, the definition is not a failed attempt to protect Muslims. It is a successful attempt to protect the state. It gives the government something to point to whenever anti-Muslim hatred makes headlines, while ensuring that the policies most responsible for institutionalising Islamophobia remain beyond its reach.

A serious response would begin where the definition refuses to look, with the counterterrorism architecture itself. Prevent and the powers built alongside it must be abolished. Until then, any definition written by the state will describe the problem in a way that leaves the state out of it.
